claim: Over a billion humans are infected with soil-transmitted helminths (STHs).
source: Over a billion humans are infected with an STH — the roundworm Ascaris lumbricoides, the whipworm Trichuris trichuria, and the hookworm Necator americanus account for most of these infections (WHO Expert Committee on the Control of Schistosomiasis, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO Expert Committee on the Control of Schistosomiasis, 2002

claim: Ascaris lumbricoides, Trichuris trichuria, and Necator americanus account for most STH infections.
source: Over a billion humans are infected with an STH — the roundworm Ascaris lumbricoides, the whipworm Trichuris trichuria, and the hookworm Necator americanus account for most of these infections (WHO Expert Committee on the Control of Schistosomiasis, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO Expert Committee on the Control of Schistosomiasis, 2002

claim: STHs are transmitted from human to human via soil where eggs from human faeces develop into infective stages.
source: STHs are transmitted from human to human via the soil where eggs from human faeces develop into infective stages which then enter new hosts (reviewed in Brooker et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brooker et al., 2006

claim: Oxygen levels in the host intestine drop steeply to near anoxia in the lumen.
source: While there is abundant oxygen outside their hosts, in many host tissues there is little available oxygen — this is especially true in the intestine where oxygen levels drop steeply to near anoxia in the lumen (reviewed in Espey, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Espey, 2013

claim: The anaerobic metabolic pathways that STHs depend on are unusual and are not used in any host.
source: crucially, the anaerobic metabolic pathways that STHs depend on are unusual and are not used in any host (Van Hellemond et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to Van Hellemond et al., 1995

claim: During aerobic respiration in helminths, the great majority of ATP is made in the mitochondrion.
source: During aerobic respiration in helminths, the great majority of ATP is made in the mitochondrion (Tielens, 1994; Tielens et al., 1984).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tielens, 1994 and Tielens et al., 1984

claim: Electrons enter the Electron Transport Chain either at Complex I or via several quinone-coupled dehydrogenases.
source: Electrons enter the Electron Transport Chain (ETC) either at Complex I or via several quinone-coupled dehydrogenases (QDHs from here on).
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript text

claim: Quinone-coupled dehydrogenases include Succinate Dehydrogenase (Complex II) and Electron-Transferring Flavoprotein Dehydrogenase (ETFDH).
source: These QDHs include Succinate Dehydrogenase (Complex II) and Electron-Transferring Flavoprotein Dehydrogenase (ETFDH) (Komuniecki et al., 1989; Ma et al., 1993; Rioux and Komuniecki, 1984).
evidence: Supported by citations to Komuniecki et al., 1989; Ma et al., 1993; Rioux and Komuniecki, 1984

claim: Electrons entering the ETC are first transferred to ubiquinone (UQ).
source: The electrons entering the ETC are first transferred to the lipid soluble electron carrier ubiquinone (UQ) (Crane et al., 1957; Mitchell, 1975).
evidence: Supported by citations to Crane et al., 1957 and Mitchell, 1975

claim: From UQ, electrons are ultimately carried to Complex III then IV where they are transferred onto oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor.
source: From UQ, they are ultimately carried to Complex III then IV where they are finally transferred onto oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor (see Figure 1a).
evidence: Direct statement in text with reference to Figure 1a

claim: Electron transport is coupled to proton pumping into the inner membrane space of the mitochondrion.
source: Electron transport is coupled to proton pumping into the inner membrane space of the mitochondrion — this establishes a proton gradient which is used to power the F0F1-ATP synthase (Mitchell, 1961).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mitchell, 1961

claim: When there is insufficient oxygen, almost all animals stop using the ETC and rely on anaerobic glycolysis to make ATP, generating lactate.
source: When there is insufficient oxygen to accept electrons at Complex IV, or when inhibitors of Complex IV such as cyanide are present (Antonini et al., 1971; Nicholls et al., 1972), almost all animals stop using the ETC and rely on anaerobic glycolysis to make ATP, generating lactate (Isom et al., 1975; Meyerhof, 1927).
evidence: Supported by citations to Antonini et al., 1971; Nicholls et al., 1972; Isom et al., 1975; Meyerhof, 1927

claim: STHs have evolved a different solution that allows them to survive months in the hypoxic host environment.
source: STHs, however, have evolved a different solution that allow them to survive months in the hypoxic host environment.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript

claim: In STHs under anaerobic conditions, electrons still enter the ETC at Complex I and Complex I still pumps protons.
source: Electrons still enter the ETC at Complex I, Complex I still pumps protons to generate the proton motive force (PMF), and ATP is still made by the F0F1ATPase, powered by the PMF.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript

claim: In STHs under anaerobic conditions, electrons exit the ETC immediately downstream of Complex I onto alternative terminal electron acceptors.
source: However, rather than the electrons passing through the ETC to oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor, they exit the ETC immediately downstream of Complex I onto a number of alternative terminal electron acceptors (Figure 1b) (reviewed in Hochachka and Mustafa, 1972; Müller et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hochachka and Mustafa, 1972 and Müller et al., 2012, with reference to Figure 1b

claim: Transfer of electrons out of the ETC onto alternative electron acceptors requires quinone-coupled dehydrogenases.
source: This transfer of the electrons out of the ETC and onto alternative electron acceptors requires the quinone-coupled dehydrogenases (Kita, 1992; Ma et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kita, 1992 and Ma et al., 1993

claim: Under aerobic conditions, QDHs act as entry points to the ETC, transferring electrons from their substrates to UQ.
source: Under aerobic conditions these QDHs act as entry points to the ETC, transferring electrons from their substrates to UQ.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript

claim: The reactions catalysed by QDHs are reversed in anaerobic conditions.
source: Crucially, the reactions catalysed by these QDHs are reversed in anaerobic conditions — they now act as reductases transferring electrons out of the ETC and onto their products.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript

claim: Complex II acts as a succinate dehydrogenase in aerobic conditions, generating fumarate.
source: For example, Complex II acts as a succinate dehydrogenase in aerobic conditions, generating fumarate; in anaerobic conditions, it reduces fumarate generating succinate as a terminal electron sink (Figure 1c) (Kmetec and Bueding, 1961; Sato et al., 1972; Saz and Vidrine, 1959; Van Hellemond et al., 1995; Takamiya et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kmetec and Bueding, 1961; Sato et al., 1972; Saz and Vidrine, 1959; Van Hellemond et al., 1995; Takamiya et al., 1999, with reference to Figure 1c

claim: In anaerobic conditions, Complex II reduces fumarate generating succinate as a terminal electron sink.
source: For example, Complex II acts as a succinate dehydrogenase in aerobic conditions, generating fumarate; in anaerobic conditions, it reduces fumarate generating succinate as a terminal electron sink (Figure 1c) (Kmetec and Bueding, 1961; Sato et al., 1972; Saz and Vidrine, 1959; Van Hellemond et al., 1995; Takamiya et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kmetec and Bueding, 1961; Sato et al., 1972; Saz and Vidrine, 1959; Van Hellemond et al., 1995; Takamiya et al., 1999, with reference to Figure 1c

claim: The unusual ETC wiring used by STHs to survive anaerobic conditions requires rhodoquinone (RQ).
source: The unusual ETC wiring used by STHs to survive anaerobic conditions requires an unusual electron carrier, rhodoquinone (RQ) (Moore and Folkers, 1965).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moore and Folkers, 1965

claim: The sole difference between RQ and UQ is the presence of an amine group on the quinone ring of RQ.
source: RQ and UQ are highly related molecules — the sole difference is the presence of an amine group on the quinone ring of RQ (Figure 1d).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 1d showing molecular structures

claim: UQ can accept electrons from QDHs as they flow into the ETC under aerobic conditions.
source: while UQ can accept electrons from the QDHs as they flow into the ETC under aerobic conditions, UQ cannot carry electrons of the correct electropotential to drive the reverse reactions in anaerobic conditions (Fioravanti and Kim, 1988; Sato et al., 1972).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fioravanti and Kim, 1988 and Sato et al., 1972

claim: UQ cannot carry electrons of the correct electropotential to drive the reverse reactions in anaerobic conditions.
source: while UQ can accept electrons from the QDHs as they flow into the ETC under aerobic conditions, UQ cannot carry electrons of the correct electropotential to drive the reverse reactions in anaerobic conditions (Fioravanti and Kim, 1988; Sato et al., 1972).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fioravanti and Kim, 1988 and Sato et al., 1972

claim: RQ can carry electrons of the correct electropotential to drive reverse reactions in anaerobic conditions.
source: RQ can carry such electrons (Fioravanti and Kim, 1988; Sato et al., 1972), however, and the ability of STHs to drive their unusual anaerobic metabolism in their hosts is absolutely dependent on RQ.
evidence: Supported by citations to Fioravanti and Kim, 1988 and Sato et al., 1972

claim: The ability of STHs to drive their unusual anaerobic metabolism in their hosts is absolutely dependent on RQ.
source: RQ can carry such electrons (Fioravanti and Kim, 1988; Sato et al., 1972), however, and the ability of STHs to drive their unusual anaerobic metabolism in their hosts is absolutely dependent on RQ.
evidence: Supported by citations to Fioravanti and Kim, 1988 and Sato et al., 1972

claim: RQ is found in very few animal species — only helminths, molluscs and annelids are known to make RQ.
source: RQ is found in very few animal species — only helminths, molluscs and annelids are known to make RQ (Allen, 1973; Fioravanti and Kim, 1988; Sato and Ozawa, 1969; Takamiya et al., 1999; Van Hellemond et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Allen, 1973; Fioravanti and Kim, 1988; Sato and Ozawa, 1969; Takamiya et al., 1999; Van Hellemond et al., 1995

claim: No host animals make RQ.
source: Since no host animals make RQ, inhibiting RQ synthesis or RQ use is a potentially powerful way to target parasites inside their host.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript

claim: In R.rubrum, RQ appears to derive from UQ.
source: The most mature studies have focused on the purple Proteobacterium R.rubrum, where RQ appears to derive from UQ (Brajcich et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brajcich et al., 2010

claim: RQ synthesis in R.rubrum requires the gene rquA.
source: RQ synthesis in R.rubrum requires the gene rquA (Lonjers et al., 2012) which is the first and thus far only gene known to be required for RQ synthesis in any organism.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lonjers et al., 2012

claim: rquA is the first and only gene known to be required for RQ synthesis in any organism.
source: RQ synthesis in R.rubrum requires the gene rquA (Lonjers et al., 2012) which is the first and thus far only gene known to be required for RQ synthesis in any organism.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lonjers et al., 2012

claim: rquA is capable of converting UQ to RQ.
source: The role of rquA was initially unclear (Lonjers et al., 2012), but very recently it has emerged that it is capable of converting UQ to RQ (Bernert et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bernert et al., 2019

claim: There are no clear rquA orthologues in animals.
source: In animals, the situation is even more blank: nothing is known about which genes are required for RQ synthesis, there are no clear rquA orthologues (Lonjers et al., 2012), and there are no drugs that are known to prevent RQ synthesis.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lonjers et al., 2012

claim: There are no drugs known to prevent RQ synthesis.
source: In animals, the situation is even more blank: nothing is known about which genes are required for RQ synthesis, there are no clear rquA orthologues (Lonjers et al., 2012), and there are no drugs that are known to prevent RQ synthesis.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript

claim: C. elegans can make RQ.
source: Previous studies have shown that C. elegans, a free-living helminth, can make RQ (Takamiya et al., 1999) and that when C. elegans is exposed to hypoxic conditions it undergoes major metabolic changes that resemble those that occur in STHs when they are in the hypoxic environment of their hosts (Butler et al., 2012; Föll et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Takamiya et al., 1999

claim: When C. elegans is exposed to hypoxic conditions it undergoes major metabolic changes that resemble those in STHs in their hosts.
source: Previous studies have shown that C. elegans, a free-living helminth, can make RQ (Takamiya et al., 1999) and that when C. elegans is exposed to hypoxic conditions it undergoes major metabolic changes that resemble those that occur in STHs when they are in the hypoxic environment of their hosts (Butler et al., 2012; Föll et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Butler et al., 2012 and Föll et al., 1999

claim: C. elegans makes both UQ and RQ when maintained in normoxic conditions.
source: We extracted quinones as described in Materials and methods and as shown in Figure 2a and Supp Figure 1, C. elegans makes both UQ and RQ when maintained in normoxic conditions.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a and Supplementary Figure 1

claim: C. elegans increases succinate production following treatment with Potassium Cyanide (KCN).
source: C. elegans L1 larvae were treated either with 200 µM KCN alone, 12.5 µM rotenone alone, or a combination of KCN and rotenone for 1 hr and metabolites extracted and analysed by mass spectrometry (see Materials and methods). The graph shows that succinate levels increase over 5-fold following KCN treatment and that this increase is blocked by rotenone indicating that it requires Complex I activity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b

claim: The increase in succinate following KCN treatment is blocked by rotenone, indicating it requires Complex I activity.
source: The graph shows that succinate levels increase over 5-fold following KCN treatment and that this increase is blocked by rotenone indicating that it requires Complex I activity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b

claim: When C. elegans are exposed to KCN, they build up high levels of succinate.
source: We found that when C. elegans are exposed to KCN, they build up high levels of succinate as expected and that inhibiting Complex I with rotenone prevents succinate build-up (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b

claim: Inhibiting Complex I with rotenone prevents succinate build-up in C. elegans exposed to KCN.
source: We found that when C. elegans are exposed to KCN, they build up high levels of succinate as expected and that inhibiting Complex I with rotenone prevents succinate build-up (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b

claim: Treatment of C. elegans with KCN causes them to switch to a metabolic state that resembles that of STHs in their host.
source: We thus find that C. elegans makes RQ and that treatment of C. elegans with KCN causes them to switch to a metabolic state that resembles that of STHs in their host.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data showing succinate accumulation

claim: In R.rubrum, RQ is made by a late addition of the critical amine group to an existing molecule of UQ.
source: At least in this prokaryote, RQ is thought to be made by a late addition of the critical amine group to an existing molecule of UQ (Brajcich et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brajcich et al., 2010

claim: In R.rubrum, UQ is an obligate precursor of RQ.
source: UQ is thus an obligate precursor of RQ and RQ synthesis requires initial synthesis of UQ (Figure 3a).
evidence: Based on inference from bacterial RQ synthesis pathway with reference to Figure 3a

claim: The clk-1(qm30) strain has a loss-of-function mutation in the C. elegans COQ7 orthologue.
source: The clk-1(qm30) strain has a loss-of-function mutation in the C. elegans COQ7 orthologue that is required for hydroxylation of 5-demethoxyubiquinone to 5-hydroxyubiquinone, a late step in UQ synthesis — there is no detectable UQ in clk-1(qm30) homozygous animals.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript

claim: There is no detectable UQ in clk-1(qm30) homozygous animals.
source: The clk-1(qm30) strain has a loss-of-function mutation in the C. elegans COQ7 orthologue that is required for hydroxylation of 5-demethoxyubiquinone to 5-hydroxyubiquinone, a late step in UQ synthesis — there is no detectable UQ in clk-1(qm30) homozygous animals.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript

claim: There is RQ in the clk-1(qm30) strain.
source: However, a previous study showed that there does appear to be RQ in this strain (Jonassen et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jonassen et al., 2001

claim: While there is no detectable UQ in clk-1(qm30) mutants, there is abundant RQ and RQ levels are essentially unchanged.
source: We find that while there is no detectable UQ in clk-1(qm30) mutants, there is abundant RQ and indeed we find that RQ levels are essentially unchanged (Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b

claim: UQ is not an obligate precursor for RQ in C. elegans.
source: We thus confirm that UQ is not an obligate precursor for RQ in C. elegans.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data showing RQ presence in UQ-deficient mutants

claim: Yeast COQ2 is able to use a variety of similar compounds as substrates for prenylation such as para-aminobenzoic acid and vanillic acid.
source: PHB has no amine group — however, S. cerevisiae COQ2 is known to be able to use a variety of similar compounds as substrates for prenylation such as para-aminobenzoic acid and vanillic acid (reviewed in Pierrel, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pierrel, 2017

claim: Yeast COQ2 is tolerant of substituents at positions 5 and 6 of the PHB structure.
source: In particular, we noted that yeast COQ2 is tolerant of substituents at positions 5 and 6 of the PHB structure (reviewed in Pierrel, 2017) suggesting that this might be feasible enzymatically.
evidence: Supported by citation to Pierrel, 2017

claim: Anthranilate and 3-hydroxyanthranilate (3 HA) are made from the amino acid tryptophan via the kynurenine pathway.
source: Anthranilate and 3 HA are made from the amino acid tryptophan via the kynurenine pathway (Heidelberger and Gullberg, 1948; Kotake, 1936) and kynu-1 encodes the C. elegans kynureninase that is required for the generation of anthranilate and 3 HA (Babu, 1974; Bhat and Babu, 1980; van der Goot et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Heidelberger and Gullberg, 1948 and Kotake, 1936

claim: kynu-1 encodes the C. elegans kynureninase that is required for the generation of anthranilate and 3 HA.
source: Anthranilate and 3 HA are made from the amino acid tryptophan via the kynurenine pathway (Heidelberger and Gullberg, 1948; Kotake, 1936) and kynu-1 encodes the C. elegans kynureninase that is required for the generation of anthranilate and 3 HA (Babu, 1974; Bhat and Babu, 1980; van der Goot et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Babu, 1974; Bhat and Babu, 1980; van der Goot et al., 2012

claim: While UQ levels are normal in the kynu-1(e1003) mutant animals, there is no detectable RQ.
source: We examined the quinones present in kynu-1(e1003) mutants that lack kynureninase and while UQ levels are normal in the kynu-1(e1003) mutant animals, there is no detectable RQ (Figure 3c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c

claim: The amine group on RQ derives from anthranilate or 3 HA, or some closely related product of kynureninase.
source: This suggests that the amine group on RQ derives from anthranilate or 3 HA, or some closely related product of kynureninase.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data showing loss of RQ in kynu-1 mutants

claim: afmd-1 encodes a kynurenine formamidase.
source: These contain loss-of-function mutations in either afmd-1, which encodes a kynurenine formamidase, or in kmo-1 which encodes a kynurenine 3-monoxygenase.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript

claim: kmo-1 encodes a kynurenine 3-monoxygenase.
source: These contain loss-of-function mutations in either afmd-1, which encodes a kynurenine formamidase, or in kmo-1 which encodes a kynurenine 3-monoxygenase.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript

claim: The afmd-1(tm4547) strain cannot make either anthranilate or 3 HA.
source: Based on current models for the kynurenine pathway, afmd-1(tm4547) strain cannot make either anthranilate or 3 HA whereas the kmo-1(tm4529) can generate anthranilate but not 3 HA.
evidence: Based on inference from known kynurenine pathway models

claim: The kmo-1(tm4529) strain can generate anthranilate but not 3 HA.
source: Based on current models for the kynurenine pathway, afmd-1(tm4547) strain cannot make either anthranilate or 3 HA whereas the kmo-1(tm4529) can generate anthranilate but not 3 HA.
evidence: Based on inference from known kynurenine pathway models

claim: Both afmd-1(tm4547) and kmo-1(tm4529) strains have reduced RQ levels compared with N2.
source: We find that both strains have reduced RQ levels compared with N2 (Figure 3d) suggesting that the key precursor is 3 HA.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3d

claim: The key precursor for RQ is 3 HA.
source: We find that both strains have reduced RQ levels compared with N2 (Figure 3d) suggesting that the key precursor is 3 HA.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data in Figure 3d

claim: A m/z peak corresponding to the predicted mass of prenylated 3 HA was identified.
source: Consistent with this, we identify a m/z peak corresponding to the predicted mass of prenylated 3 HA (Supp Figure 2), but find no equivalent peak for prenylated anthranilate (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Supplementary Figure 2

claim: No equivalent peak for prenylated anthranilate was found.
source: Consistent with this, we identify a m/z peak corresponding to the predicted mass of prenylated 3 HA (Supp Figure 2), but find no equivalent peak for prenylated anthranilate (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by experimental data (data not shown)

claim: RQ synthesis requires the kynurenine pathway to generate 3 HA.
source: Both the genetic data and mass spec data thus show that RQ synthesis requires the kynurenine pathway to generate 3 HA and that 3 HA is a substrate for COQ-2.
evidence: Based on inference from genetic and mass spectrometry data

claim: 3 HA is a substrate for COQ-2.
source: Both the genetic data and mass spec data thus show that RQ synthesis requires the kynurenine pathway to generate 3 HA and that 3 HA is a substrate for COQ-2.
evidence: Based on inference from genetic and mass spectrometry data

claim: When worms are fed with 15N bacteria alone, the RQ detected is approximately all 15N labelled.
source: As expected, the RQ detected in animals fed with 15N bacteria alone is approximately all 15N labelled (Figure 4b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b

claim: If 14N tryptophan was added while worms are feeding on 15N-labelled bacteria, ~50% of the RQ observed was 14N RQ.
source: However, if 14N tryptophan was added while worms are feeding on the 15N-labelled bacteria,~50% of the RQ observed was 14N RQ — the sole source for this 14N was the added tryptophan (Figure 4b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b

claim: The sole source of 14N in RQ when 14N tryptophan is added is the added tryptophan.
source: However, if 14N tryptophan was added while worms are feeding on the 15N-labelled bacteria,~50% of the RQ observed was 14N RQ — the sole source for this 14N was the added tryptophan (Figure 4b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b

claim: If 14N 3 HA is added instead of 14N Trp, significant 14N RQ is detected.
source: We note that if we add 14N 3 HA instead of 14N Trp we also detect significant 14N RQ, but see no 14N RQ if 14N anthranilate is added, further confirming that 3 HA is the key RQ precursor (Figure 4c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c

claim: No 14N RQ is detected if 14N anthranilate is added.
source: We note that if we add 14N 3 HA instead of 14N Trp we also detect significant 14N RQ, but see no 14N RQ if 14N anthranilate is added, further confirming that 3 HA is the key RQ precursor (Figure 4c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c

claim: RQ does not derive from UQ.
source: Taken together, our data suggest that RQ does not derive from UQ, and that 3 HA is the source of the amine group on the quinone ring of RQ.
evidence: Based on inference from multiple experimental results

claim: 3 HA is the source of the amine group on the quinone ring of RQ.
source: Taken together, our data suggest that RQ does not derive from UQ, and that 3 HA is the source of the amine group on the quinone ring of RQ.
evidence: Based on inference from multiple experimental results

claim: The pathway of RQ and UQ synthesis are largely the same — the key difference is the presence or absence of the amine group on the initial aromatic ring substrate for COQ-2.
source: We propose that the pathway of RQ and UQ synthesis are largely the same — the key difference is the presence or absence of the amine group on the initial aromatic ring substrate for COQ-2.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental results and pathway analysis

claim: While wild-type worms generate high levels of succinate when Complex IV is inhibited with KCN, RQ-deficient kynu-1(e1003) mutant animals do not.
source: While wild-type worms generate high levels of succinate when Complex IV is inhibited with KCN, RQ-deficient kynu-1(e1003) mutant animals do not (Figure 5), confirming that the metabolic shift we see when we expose C. elegans to KCN is not simply similar to that of parasitic helminths in their hosts, it also requires RQ.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5

claim: The metabolic shift when C. elegans is exposed to KCN requires RQ.
source: While wild-type worms generate high levels of succinate when Complex IV is inhibited with KCN, RQ-deficient kynu-1(e1003) mutant animals do not (Figure 5), confirming that the metabolic shift we see when we expose C. elegans to KCN is not simply similar to that of parasitic helminths in their hosts, it also requires RQ.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 5

claim: There is no significant difference in acute KCN sensitivity between wild-type worms and kynu-1(e1003) mutants.
source: We found no significant differences in acute KCN sensitivity of wild-type worms and kynu-1(e1003) mutants — both slow their movement in the presence of KCN, stop moving completely by ~90 min (Figure 6a), and remain immobile from there on when maintained in KCN.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6a

claim: Both wild-type and kynu-1(e1003) mutants slow their movement in the presence of KCN and stop moving completely by ~90 min.
source: We found no significant differences in acute KCN sensitivity of wild-type worms and kynu-1(e1003) mutants — both slow their movement in the presence of KCN, stop moving completely by ~90 min (Figure 6a), and remain immobile from there on when maintained in KCN.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6a

claim: When wild-type worms are removed from KCN, they rapidly recover movement.
source: When wild-type worms are removed from KCN, they rapidly recover movement (Figure 6b; recovery is also shown as a movie in Video 1) — they can do this even after 24 hr of KCN treatment (Figure 6c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6b and Video 1

claim: Wild-type worms can recover movement even after 24 hr of KCN treatment.
source: When wild-type worms are removed from KCN, they rapidly recover movement (Figure 6b; recovery is also shown as a movie in Video 1) — they can do this even after 24 hr of KCN treatment (Figure 6c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6c

claim: kynu-1(e1003) mutants show greatly reduced ability to survive extended KCN treatment.
source: However, kynu-1(e1003) mutants show greatly reduced ability to survive extended KCN treatment — they do not survive exposure to KCN for 12 hr or more (Figure 6c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6c

claim: kynu-1(e1003) mutants do not survive exposure to KCN for 12 hr or more.
source: However, kynu-1(e1003) mutants show greatly reduced ability to survive extended KCN treatment — they do not survive exposure to KCN for 12 hr or more (Figure 6c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6c

claim: RQ-dependent anaerobic metabolism allows C. elegans to survive extended periods where it cannot use oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor of the ETC.
source: RQ-dependent anaerobic metabolism thus allows C. elegans to survive extended periods where it cannot use oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor of the ETC.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data showing differential survival of wild-type vs kynu-1 mutants

claim: wact-11 is a Complex II inhibitor that binds to the quinone-binding pocket of Complex II.
source: To test this, we used the compound wact-11 — this is a Complex II inhibitor that binds to the quinone-binding pocket of Complex II (Burns et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Burns et al., 2015

claim: wact-11 is highly related to the anthelmintic flutolanil.
source: wact-11 is highly related to the anthelmintic flutolanil (Burns et al., 2015) and is highly selective for helminth Complex II (Burns et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Burns et al., 2015

claim: wact-11 is highly selective for helminth Complex II.
source: wact-11 is highly related to the anthelmintic flutolanil (Burns et al., 2015) and is highly selective for helminth Complex II (Burns et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Burns et al., 2015

claim: When worms are treated with wact-11 alone, there is no impact on worm movement over the time course of the assay.
source: When worms are treated with wact-11 alone, we see no impact on worm movement over the time course of our assay.
evidence: Supported by experimental observation

claim: When worms are treated with both wact-11 and KCN, they can no longer survive long-term KCN exposure.
source: However, when worms are treated with both wact-11 and KCN, they can no longer survive long-term KCN exposure (Figure 6d) indicating that this assay can allow discovery of drugs that block RQ-dependent anaerobic metabolism.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6d

claim: Mutations that result in resistance to wact-11 treatment cluster in the quinone binding pocket of Complex II.
source: Mutations that result in resistance to wact-11 treatment cluster in the quinone binding pocket of Complex II (Burns et al., 2015) and we reasoned that some of these might not only prevent the binding of wact-11 but might fortuitously also disrupt the binding of RQ and thus affect the ability of worms to survive extended exposure to KCN.
evidence: Supported by citation to Burns et al., 2015

claim: The G71E mutation results in worms that are unable to survive extended KCN exposure.
source: However, we found that the G71E mutation results in worms that are unable to survive extended KCN exposure — the G71E animals thus resemble kynu-1(e1003) mutants.
evidence: Supported by experimental observation

claim: The G71E mutation sits right above the modelled binding site for the rhodoquinone ring.
source: We note that this mutation sits right above the modelled binding site for the rhodoquinone ring, whereas a neighbouring mutation that sits two turns of an alpha-helix further away (C78Y) has no effect.
evidence: Based on structural modeling analysis

claim: The C78Y mutation has no effect on ability to survive extended KCN exposure.
source: We note that this mutation sits right above the modelled binding site for the rhodoquinone ring, whereas a neighbouring mutation that sits two turns of an alpha-helix further away (C78Y) has no effect.
evidence: Supported by experimental observation

claim: The G71E mutation affects the ability of C. elegans to bind RQ into the quinone binding pocket of Complex II.
source: We thus suggest that the G71E mutation affects the ability of C. elegans to bind RQ into the quinone binding pocket of Complex II and thus to drive RQ-dependent fumarate reduction as part of its RQ-dependent anaerobic metabolism.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data and structural analysis

claim: RQ was first identified over 50 years ago.
source: RQ was first identified over 50 years ago (Moore and Folkers, 1965).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moore and Folkers, 1965

claim: RQ is absolutely required for the anaerobic metabolism used by parasitic helminths to survive in the hypoxic environment of the host gut.
source: It is absolutely required for the anaerobic metabolism used by parasitic helminths to survive in the hypoxic environment of the host gut where they can thrive for many months.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript

claim: The single amine group on RQ allows it to carry electrons of the right electropotential to drive quinone-coupled dehydrogenases in reverse.
source: The single amine group that differs between RQ and UQ is crucial for this — it allows RQ to carry electrons of the right electropotential to drive quinone-coupled dehydrogenases (QDHs) in reverse, acting as reductases (Fioravanti and Kim, 1988; Sato et al., 1972).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fioravanti and Kim, 1988 and Sato et al., 1972

claim: In bacteria, RQ synthesis requires UQ synthesis and the key amine group is a late stage addition.
source: Very recently, RquA has been shown to be able to catalyse the conversion of UQ to RQ (Buceta et al., 2019)— in bacteria, RQ synthesis thus requires UQ synthesis and the key amine group is a late stage addition.
evidence: Supported by citation to Buceta et al., 2019

claim: In C. elegans, RQ synthesis does not require UQ as a precursor.
source: Here, however, we show that the mechanism of RQ synthesis in C. elegans is different. In C. elegans (and likely in helminths in general) RQ synthesis does not require UQ as a precursor and, crucially, the critical amine group on the quinone ring of RQ is not added at a late stage in the synthesis of RQ but is present from the initial steps of RQ synthesis.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental results showing RQ in UQ-deficient mutants

claim: In C. elegans, the critical amine group on the quinone ring of RQ is present from the initial steps of RQ synthesis.
source: In C. elegans (and likely in helminths in general) RQ synthesis does not require UQ as a precursor and, crucially, the critical amine group on the quinone ring of RQ is not added at a late stage in the synthesis of RQ but is present from the initial steps of RQ synthesis.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental results with isotope labeling and kynurenine pathway mutants

claim: The amine group on RQ likely comes from 3-hydroxyanthranilate (3 HA), which is generated by degradation of tryptophan via the kynurenine pathway.
source: We show that the amine group likely comes from 3-hydroxyanthranilate (3 HA), which is generated by degradation of tryptophan via the kynurenine pathway.
evidence: Based on inference from genetic and isotope labeling experiments

claim: During revision of the manuscript, a second group also found that RQ synthesis requires the kynurenine pathway.
source: We note that during revision of the manuscript, a second group also found that RQ synthesis requires the kynurenine pathway (Buceta et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Buceta et al., 2019

claim: UQ and RQ have a largely shared synthesis pathway.
source: First, we do not believe that there are completely separate dedicated pathways for UQ and for RQ synthesis in helminths. Instead, we suggest that UQ and RQ have a largely shared synthesis pathway.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental results and pathway analysis

claim: A key difference in RQ and UQ synthesis is the use of different initial substrates for the polyprenyltransferase COQ-2.
source: A key difference in RQ and UQ synthesis is the use of different initial substrates for the polyprenyltransferase COQ-2. If PHB is used, the product will be UQ; if 3 HA (or possibly a related product of tryptophan metabolism) is used, the product will be RQ.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental results

claim: Facultative anaerobic bacteria including E. coli and M. tuberculosis make two quinones: UQ and menaquinone (MK).
source: Facultative anaerobic bacteria including non-pathogenic E. coli as well as major human pathogens like M. tuberculosis make two quinones: UQ which is used as an electron carrier under aerobic conditions, and menaquinone (MK) (reviewed in Meganathan and Kwon, 2009), which acts as a carrier under anaerobic conditions.
evidence: Supported by citation to Meganathan and Kwon, 2009

claim: The synthesis pathways of UQ and MK in bacteria are completely distinct.
source: The synthesis pathways of UQ and MK are completely distinct and the genes involved are distinct (reviewed in Meganathan and Kwon, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Meganathan and Kwon, 2009

claim: There may be no dedicated RQ synthesis pathway in helminths analogous to the dedicated MK synthesis pathway in bacteria.
source: We suggest that there may be no analogous inhibitors for 'the RQ synthesis pathway' in helminths since there does not appear to be a dedicated RQ pathway analogous to the dedicated MK synthesis pathway.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental results and comparison with bacterial systems

claim: The human gut is likely to be a source of anthranilate and 3 HA from host metabolism or from the microbiome.
source: However, the human gut is likely to be a source of anthranilate and 3 HA from host metabolism or from the microbiome and inhibiting production of these molecules in the helminth itself might thus prove ineffective.
evidence: Based on speculation about potential drug targets

claim: The host only makes UQ and not RQ, whereas the parasite COQ-2 must be able to use both PHB for UQ synthesis and amine-containing precursors like 3 HA for RQ synthesis.
source: While host and parasite COQ-2 are orthologous enzymes, they have different substrate specificity: the host only makes UQ and not RQ, whereas the parasite COQ-2 must be able to use not only PHB for UQ synthesis but also amine-containing precursors like 3 HA for RQ synthesis.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental results and known biology

claim: The ability of helminth COQ-2 to use amine-containing substrates efficiently opens up the possibility of helminth-specific COQ-2 inhibitors.
source: The ability of helminth COQ-2 to use amine-containing substrates efficiently thus opens up the possibility of helminth-specific COQ-2 inhibitors, a potential avenue for new anthelmintics.
evidence: Based on speculation about potential drug development

claim: TDO-2 and KMO-1 in the kynurenine pathway are monooxygenases or dioxygenases that require oxygen.
source: These include TDO-2 (Hayaishi et al., 1957) and KMO-1 (Detmer and Massey, 1985; Entsch et al., 1976) in the kynurenine pathway and COQ-6 (Ozeir et al., 2015) and CLK-1 (Marbois and Clarke, 1996) in the UQ synthesis pathway.
evidence: Supported by citations to Hayaishi et al., 1957; Detmer and Massey, 1985; Entsch et al., 1976

claim: COQ-6 and CLK-1 in the UQ synthesis pathway are monooxygenases or dioxygenases that require oxygen.
source: These include TDO-2 (Hayaishi et al., 1957) and KMO-1 (Detmer and Massey, 1985; Entsch et al., 1976) in the kynurenine pathway and COQ-6 (Ozeir et al., 2015) and CLK-1 (Marbois and Clarke, 1996) in the UQ synthesis pathway.
evidence: Supported by citations to Ozeir et al., 2015 and Marbois and Clarke, 1996

claim: RQ synthesis appears to require the availability of oxygen for oxygen-requiring enzymes.
source: RQ synthesis thus appears to require the availability of oxygen for these enzymes, an unexpected result since RQ is preferentially required in anaerobic conditions and is the predominant quinone in helminths living under anaerobic conditions.
evidence: Based on inference from known enzyme requirements

claim: Ascaris haem is octameric and binds oxygen with ~25,000 times greater affinity than human haem.
source: Other oxygen-using proteins have evolved extremely high oxygen affinity in helminths — for example Ascaris haem is octameric and binds oxygen with ~25,000 times greater affinity than human haem (Minning et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Minning et al., 1999

claim: In E. coli, under aerobic conditions UbiB and UbiF carry out the same hydroxylation modifications to the quinone ring as C. elegans COQ-6 and CLK-1.
source: In E. coli, for example, in aerobic conditions UbiB and UbiF carry out the same hydroxylation modifications to the quinone ring as C. elegans COQ-6 and CLK-1 and mutation of either gene results in a lack of mature UQ in these bacteria (reviewed in Meganathan and Kwon, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Meganathan and Kwon, 2009

claim: Under anaerobic conditions in E. coli, ubiB and ubiF mutants make normal levels of UQ.
source: However, under anaerobic conditions, ubiB and ubiF mutants make normal levels of UQ suggesting that other enzymes carry out these reactions in low oxygen conditions (Alexander and Young, 1978).
evidence: Supported by citation to Alexander and Young, 1978

claim: Resistance to known classes of anthelmintics is widespread among livestock parasites like H.contortus, C.oncophora and A.suum.
source: Since resistance to known classes of anthelmintics is widespread among livestock parasites like H.contortus, C.oncophora and A.suum and is rising in human populations (reviewed in Sangster et al., 2018), this will prove critical in the control and treatment of these major pathogens.
evidence: Supported by citation to Sangster et al., 2018

claim: Resistance to anthelmintics is rising in human populations.
source: Since resistance to known classes of anthelmintics is widespread among livestock parasites like H.contortus, C.oncophora and A.suum and is rising in human populations (reviewed in Sangster et al., 2018), this will prove critical in the control and treatment of these major pathogens.
evidence: Supported by citation to Sangster et al., 2018
